title: Growth, inflation and real returns
summary: Growth over several years is measured with CAGR, not the average of yearly rates. Inflation shrinks what money buys, so the return that matters is the real one. RRI, FVSCHEDULE and PDURATION do the arithmetic.
objectives: Measure growth over several years with CAGR, using RRI.
Grow money through different yearly returns with FVSCHEDULE.
Project future costs with inflation and work out a real return.
Find how long money takes to reach a target with PDURATION.

p: Saanjh Snacks’ revenue grew 25%, fell 10%, then grew 18%, 15% and 15%. The average of those is 12.7%, but the revenue didn’t grow 12.7% a year.
A fall needs a **bigger** rise to recover: −10% then +10% leaves you at 99%.
Growing 12.7% a year from ₹420 lakh would reach 763, not 740.
Growth over several years needs one steady rate that joins the start to the end.
In real life: told a lender his namkeen business “grows about 13% a year”, the average of his yearly rates. The lender’s analyst worked out 12.0%, and asked why the numbers differed.

slides.h: CAGR: one steady rate from start to end
p: The compound annual growth rate is the steady yearly rate that turns the first value into the last: `=RRI(5, 420, 740)` gives 12.0%.
Without RRI: `=(B7/B2)^(1/5)-1`, the same answer.
Count **periods**, not years listed: six years of data make five years of growth.
CAGR hides the bumps on the way. Show the yearly numbers too.
In real life: quotes five-year CAGRs for revenue and profit. Analysts recompute them, because the starting year chosen can flatter the result.

p: A fund returned 15%, −8%, 22%, 6% and 11%. To grow money through returns that change every year, `=FVSCHEDULE(100000, B11:B15)` multiplies by each (1 + return) in turn.
FVSCHEDULE takes a principal and a range of rates.
The order of the returns doesn’t change the end value; it changes the ride.
In real life: checks fund adverts this way: she takes the yearly returns from the fact sheet, runs FVSCHEDULE, and compares the CAGR with her deposit.

p: Prices rise, so a rupee buys less each year. A college course costing ₹15 lakh today will cost about ₹37.8 lakh in 12 years if fees rise 8% a year.
Future cost: `=FV(inflation, years, 0, -cost today)`.
Goals must be planned in **future** rupees, or the savings fall short.
Education and health costs often rise faster than general prices.
In real life: planned her son’s college on today’s fee of ₹15 lakh. Inflated at 8% for 12 years, the target is ₹37.8 lakh, more than twice what she was saving for.

slides.h: Real return: what you gain in buying power
p: A 7% deposit with 5% inflation doesn’t make you 2% richer each year. Your real return is (1.07 ÷ 1.05) − 1 = 1.90%.
Nominal minus inflation (2%) is a quick estimate; the division is exact.
If inflation is higher than your return, the real return is **negative**: you lose buying power.
Compare investments on real returns when you plan years ahead.
In real life: kept her savings in a 4% savings account through years of 6% inflation. Her balance grew every year; what it bought shrank.

slides.h: How long to reach a target: PDURATION
p: `=PDURATION(7%, 1, 2)` gives the exact years to double at 7%: 10.24. The rule of 72 said 10.3.
PDURATION(rate, present value, future value): both values positive.
It’s for a **lump sum**; with regular payments use NPER (Lesson 1.3).
RRI and PDURATION need Excel 2013 or later.
In real life: asked when revenue would pass ₹10 crore if it kept growing at 12%. `=PDURATION(12%,740,1000)`: about 2.7 years.

demo.intro: Measure Saanjh Snacks’ growth, then plan for inflation.

frames.say: Yearly growth in **C3**: `=B3/B2-1`, filled down to C7. The years bounce between −10% and +25%.
In **F3**, `=RRI(5,B2,B7)`: 12.0% a year, compounded, joins ₹420 lakh to ₹740 lakh. The average in F2 says 12.7%.
Real return in **F9**: `=(1+F7)/(1+F8)-1`. A 7% deposit with 5% inflation adds 1.9% a year of buying power.
Future cost of college in **F14**: `=FV(F12,F13,0,-F11)`: ₹15 lakh today becomes ₹37.8 lakh.

real.title: Module lab: Meera’s goal planner
steps: Download **Goal planner**. The inputs are in **B3:B8** (green): a ₹25 lakh down payment for a flat in 8 years, 6% price inflation, ₹3 lakh already saved, and a 10% expected return.
In **B11**, the cost when needed: grow B4 by inflation with **FV**. In **B12**, what the ₹3 lakh already saved grows to by then, at the expected return, with **FV**.
In **B13**, what is still to save: B11 − B12, but never below zero (`=MAX(0,B11-B12)`).
In **B14**, the monthly SIP, paid at the **start** of each month, that builds B13 by the goal: **PMT** with a minus in front so it shows positive. In **B15**, the total the SIP pays in.
In **B16**, the yearly return the ₹3 lakh would need to reach the goal on its own, with **RRI**.
Every result must point at the inputs: Sheetah changes the inputs to two other goals and checks your answers still come out right. Save as .xlsx and upload.

points: Growth over several years: **CAGR** = `=RRI(periods, start, end)`, not the average of yearly rates.
Changing yearly returns: `=FVSCHEDULE(principal, rates)`. Future costs: `=FV(inflation, years, 0, -cost)`.
**Real return** = (1 + return) ÷ (1 + inflation) − 1; **PDURATION** gives the years to reach a target.
